Contents of https://millercenter.org/president/biden/key-events:
January 20, 2021

Biden becomes president

Joe Biden is inaugurated as the 46th president of the United States.

January 24, 2021

Flurry of executive orders

In his first few days in office, President Joe Biden signs numerous executive orders, including rejoining the World Health Organization and the Paris Climate Accord, allowing transgendered people to serve in the military, and creating the Covid-19 Health Equity Task Force.

February 9, 2021

Impeachment trial begins

The US Senate begins hearing arguments in the second impeachment trial of Donald Trump.

February 13, 2021

Senate acquits Trump

The US Senate acquits former President Donald Trump in his second impeachment trial with a vote of 57 to 43.

February 27, 2021

Third Covid-19 vaccine

FDA approves a third vaccine by Johnson and Johnson for Covid-19.

March 11, 2021

American Rescue Plan

On the anniversary of the Covid-19 shutdown, President Biden signs the American Rescue Plan Act, a $1.9-trillion economic stimulus bill to combat the effects of the Covid-19 pandemic.

March 19, 2021

100 million vaccinations

The country reaches 100 million vaccinations for COVID-19, exceeding the Biden administration's goal of administering 100 million shots in the first 100 days.

March 31, 2021

The American Jobs Plan

In a speech in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, President Biden announces the details of the American Jobs Plan, which will modernize the country's infrastructure, combat the effects of climate change, and help middle-class workers.

April 28, 2021

Addresses Congress

In honor of his first 100 days in office, President Biden gives a speech to Congress. It focuses on his administration's accomplishments so far and outlines the president's legislative priorities.

May 28, 2021

January 6 commission blocked

The US Senate Republicans block a bill to create an independent commission on the January 6 Capitol riot.

June 7, 2021

Biden ends bipartisan talks

After weeks of negotiations, Biden ends bipartisan talks on an infrastructure bill after the administration and Republicans remained far apart on its details.

June 8, 2021

First trip to Europe

President Biden leaves on his first trip to Europe, which includes a meeting of the G7 and a NATO summit.

June 17, 2021

Juneteenth holiday

Joe Biden signs a bill creating a federal holiday for Juneteenth, June 19th, to commemorate the end of slavery in the United States.

July 8, 2021

Drawdown of US forces in Afghanistan

President Biden gives an update on the drawdown of US troops from Afghanistan, due to be completed in September.

August 16, 2021

Taliban take over Afghanistan

As the United States draws down the US troop presence in Afghanistan, the Taliban seize Kabul and take over the Afghan government.

August 26, 2021

Terror attacks at Afghanistan airport

Thirteen US military service members and dozens of Afghan civilians are killed at the airport in Kabul, Afghanistan, after a suicide bomber sets off explosives in a crowd of people. The ISIS-K terrorist group claims responsibility.

August 30, 2021

War in Afghanistan ends

The last US troops leave Afghanistan after a 20-year war.

November 2, 2021

Off-year elections

In off-year elections, Republican Glenn Youngkin won the Virginia governor's race, while Democrat Phil Murphy won reelection as governor in New Jersey.

November 15, 2021

Biden signs infrastructure bill

President Biden signs the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act, a $1.2 trillion bill to improve roads, bridges, public transit, as well as increased access to clean water and the internet.

December 21, 2021

Omicron variant emerges

President Biden gives a speech about a new variant of the coronavirus known as the Omicron variant and the federal government's plan to send millions of at-home tests to Americans.

January 6, 2022

Anniversary of January 6

On the one year anniversary of the January 6 Capitol riot, President Biden addresses the American people from the US Capitol.

February 22, 2022

Sanctions against Russia

After President Vladimir Putin of Russia sends troops into two separatist-held regions of Ukraine, President Biden announces US sanctions against Russia. The sanctions target Russian finances and banking.

February 24, 2022

Russian invasion of Ukraine

Russia invades Ukraine.

February 25, 2022

Supreme Court nomination

President Biden nominates Judge Ketanji Brown Jackson to the US Supreme Court.

March 8, 2022

Ban on Russian oil and gas

President Biden announces that the United States will ban imports of natural gas and oil from Russia in an attempt to put pressure on President Putin to stop the war in Ukraine.

March 23, 2022

Travel to Europe

President Biden travels to Europe in support of Ukraine. He attends an EU Summit meeting and a NATO meeting and gives a speech in Poland.

March 29, 2022

Antilynching legislation

President Biden signs the Emmett Till Antilynching Act, making lynching a federal crime.

Supreme Court confirma

Contents of https://news.gallup.com/poll/547763/biden-ends-2023-job-approval.aspx:
#### Story Highlights

* Biden’s job rating up slightly from 37% last month to 39% now
* Biden’s rating lowest of recent presidents at same point in their presidencies
* Gallup Economic Confidence Index improves from -40 to -32

WASHINGTON, D.C. -- President Joe Biden’s job approval rating is 39%, marking a slight improvement from the 37% low points in [October](https://news.gallup.com/poll/513305/democrats-ratings-biden-slip-overall-approval.aspx) and [November](https://news.gallup.com/poll/544808/poor-marks-biden-middle-east-economy-foreign-affairs.aspx) but the fifth time his rating is below 40% in 2023.

###Embeddable###

During the latest poll’s Dec. 1-20 field period, the war between Israel and Hamas continued after a late November pause in fighting, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy visited Biden at the White House to ask for the United States’ help in his country’s war with Russia, and House Republicans unanimously voted to open an impeachment inquiry into Biden.

While rank-and-file Republicans’ ratings of Biden have been firmly entrenched in the single digits since August 2021, independents’ ratings have been more variable. After hitting a record-low 27% in November, approval of Biden is up seven percentage points this month. Approval of Biden among Democrats is currently 78%, down slightly from last month’s 83%.

###Embeddable###

## **Biden’s Current Rating Worse Than Other Modern Presidents at Same Point**

Looking at the approval ratings of the past seven presidents at the same point in their first term in office, Biden’s current 39% is the lowest. Barack Obama (43%) and Donald Trump (45%) had slightly higher ratings heading into the year they sought reelection, while all of the others were above 50%.

Job approval ratings of Bill Clinton and George H.W. Bush were 51%, and Ronald Reagan and Jimmy Carter stood at 54%. Buoyed by the mid-December capture of Saddam Hussein in 2003, George W. Bush had the highest approval rating of the eight presidents (58%).

###Embeddable###

## **Economic Confidence Slightly Improved, but Still Negative**

Americans’ confidence in the economy, while still in negative territory, has improved in December.

Gallup regularly tracks Americans' ratings of national economic conditions as excellent, good, only fair or poor, as well as their views on whether the economy is getting better or worse. The combined responses are used to create the Gallup Economic Confidence Index (ECI), which has a theoretical range of +100 (if all respondents say the economy is excellent or good and that it is getting better) to -100 (if all say it is poor and getting worse).

This month, about four in five U.S. adults rate current economic conditions in the country as only fair (33%) or poor (45%), with few describing conditions as excellent (3%) or good (19%). Furthermore, 68% of Americans say the economy is getting worse, 28% say it is improving, and 4% think it is staying the same.

The resulting -32 Economic Confidence Index reading is an improvement from last month’s -40 and well above the record low of -72 in October 2008, during the Great Recession. The ECI has been in negative territory since July 2021. This month, gas prices have declined, the stock market has neared record highs, unemployment remains low, and inflation has moderated.

###Embeddable###

Although Americans’ views of the economy are modestly improved, when asked to name the most important problem facing the U.S., mentions of the economy in general (14%) and inflation specifically (12%) remain elevated. The government and immigration are also top concerns, with 16% of Americans citing each. Immigration is the top problem among Republicans, with 37% mentioning it, far more than any other issue.

## **Bottom Line**

Biden enters 2024 with a persistently low job approval rating, the worst of any modern-day president heading into a tough reelection campaign. While the economy has shown signs of improvement and Americans are a bit more optimistic about it, it remains a pressing concern. In addition to dealing with the national economy and overseeing the United States’ role in wars in Ukraine and the Middle East, Biden continues to face a crisis at the southern U.S. border. Given Republicans’ concern about the issue, Biden can expect immigration to be a central theme in the Republican presidential nominee’s campaign in 2024.

*Explore President Biden's approval ratings and compare them with those of past presidents in the* [*Gallup Presidential Job Approval Center*](https://news.gallup.com/interactives/507569/presidential-job-approval-center.aspx)*.*

tion

The US Senate confirms Judge Ketanji Brown Jackson as the first African American woman to the US Supreme Court by a vote of 53 to 47.

May 24, 2022

School shooting in Texas

In Uvalde, Texas, a gunman open fires at an elementary school, killing 19 children and 2 teachers. It is the deadliest school shooting in almost a decade.

June 2, 2022

Proposed gun control regulations

President Biden gives a speech, calling on Congress to pass a ban on assault rifles as well as other gun control measures.

June 24, 2022

Supreme Court overturns federal right to abortion

In *Dobbs v Jackson*, the US Supreme Court rules that the Constitution does not provide the right to an abortion. The decision overrules both *Roe v. Wade* (1973) and *Planned Parenthood v. Casey* (1992).

June 25, 2022

Safer Communities Act

President Biden signs the Safer Communities Act, which addresses issues related to gun safety, school safety, and mental health to try to reduce gun violence. This bill is the first major federal gun control law in decades.

July 13, 2022

Rising inflation

Inflation continues to rise, with the Consumer Price Index climbing 9.1 percent from a year earlier in June 2022.

July 31, 2022

Al Qaeda leader killed

The United States launches a drone strike in Afghanistan that kills Al Qaeda leader, Ayman al-Zawahiri.

August 9, 2022

CHIPS and Science Act

On August 9, 2022, President Joe Biden signed the CHIPS and Science Act, which appropriated $280 billion for semiconductor and chip research and manufacturing.

August 16, 2022

Inflation Reduction Act

President Biden signs the Inflation Reduction Act, which lowers health care costs and focuses on tackling the climate crisis by reducing pollution and investing in clean energy.

August 24, 2022

Student loan forgiveness

The Biden administration announces that it will cancel up to $10,000 in student debt for most borrowers, up to $20,000 for Pell Grant recipients. The US Supreme Court strikes down the program in June 2023.

September 1, 2022

Battle for the soul of the nation

In Independence Hall in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, President Biden gives a speech ahead of the midterm elections that focuses on the state of American democracy.

October 6, 2022

Marijuana pardons

President Biden pardons all people convicted of marijuana possession under federal law and asks for a review of whether marijuana should be in the same legal category as heroin and LSD.

November 8, 2022

Midterm elections

Although Republicans retook control of the House, Democrats performed better than expected in midterm elections.

November 18, 2022

Special counsel for Trump investigations

Attorney General Merrick Garland announces that the Justice Department will appoint a special counsel to investigate former President Trump in the January 6 attack and the handling of sensitive government documents.

December 13, 2022

Same-Sex Marriage Bill

Biden signs the Respect for Marriage Act into law. The bill provides federal protections for same-sex and interracial marriages.

December 29, 2022

Electoral reform

President Biden signs the Electoral Count Reform and Presidential Transition Improvement Act of 2022, election reforms designed to prevent another January 6 attack. Along with other provisions, it outlines processes for how to handle disputes over counting electoral votes and the role of the vice president.

January 12, 2023

Special Counsel appointed

After classified government documents are found in Biden's home, Attorney General Merrick Garland appoints Robert Hur as a special counsel to investigate the matter.

January 25, 2023

US tanks to Urkraine

President Biden announces that the United States will send 31 battle tanks to Ukraine to help them defeat the Russian invasion.

February 4, 2023

Chinese balloon shot down

President Biden orders military aircraft to shoot down a high-altitude balloon from China that has flown over the country.

February 20, 2023

Visit to Ukraine

After a secret journey, President Biden arrives in Kyiv, Ukraine, to meet with President Volodymyr Zelensky. It is the first time a modern-day president ventured into a war zone that was not held by American forces.

March 20, 2023

First veto

President Biden issues the first veto of his presidency. He vetoes a bill that would ban the government from considering environmental impacts when making investments for retirement plans.

April 25, 2023

Reelection campaign

President Biden announces his campaign for reelection for a second term as president.

May 28, 2023

Debt ceiling deal reached

President Biden and Speaker of the House Kevin McCarthy reached a deal to raise the nation's debt ceiling and avoid an historic government default.

June 29, 2023

US Supreme Court ends affirmative action

The US Supreme Court rules that colleges and universities cannot used race-based affirmative action in admissions.

August 21, 2023

Trip to Maui after wildfire devestation

President and First Lady Biden trave

l to Maui, Hawaii, to tour the devestation from a wildfire on the island. A few hundred people died after the fires spread through the town of Lahaina.

September 21, 2023

Office of Gun Violence Prevention

President Biden announces the creation of the White House Office of Gun Violence Prevention.

September 26, 2023

Biden visits striking workers

President Biden visits members of the United Auto Workers union who are striking to show his support for organized labor. It is the first time a modern president has joined a picket line.

October 3, 2023

Speaker of House ousted

Far-right Republicans oust Speaker Kevin McCarthy (R-Calif) because of ideological differences. It is the first time in US history that members of the House remove the Speaker of the House in the middle of his term.

October 7, 2023

Israel declares war

Hamas, a militant Palestinian organization that runs the government in the Gaza Strip, launches a surprise attack into Israeli territory and settlements near the Gaza border, killing more than 1,200 people and seizing some 250 hostages. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel declares war against Hamas.

October 18, 2023

Biden travels to Israel

President Biden travels to Israel to signal US support for the Israelis after the Hamas attack.

October 25, 2023

Speaker elected

Representative Mike Johnson of Lousiana is elected Speaker of the House.

October 30, 2023

Executive order on artificial intelligence

President Biden signs an executive order on artificial intelligence that attempts to protect Americans from the risks of AI.

November 15, 2023

APEC Summit meeting

President Biden attends the APEC Summit meeting in San Francisco, California. The day before the meeting begins, he meets with President Xi Jinping of China.

November 20, 2023

President's birthday

President Biden celebrates his 81st birthday, making him the oldest US president in American history.

November 28, 2023

Funeral for First Lady Rosalynn Carter

President and First Lady Biden attend the funeral of Rosalynn Carter, wife of President Jimmy Carter, in Georgia.

December 12, 2023

Meeting with President of Ukraine

President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine meets with President Biden at the White House.

January 5, 2024

Campaign begins

The day before the third anniversary of the January 6th attack on the US Capitol, President Biden gives a campaign speech in Pennsylvania, laying out his case for reelection.

February 3, 2024

US strikes in Middle East

After drone attacks in Jordan kill three US soldiers, the United States carries out aerial strikes in Syria, Yemen, and Iraq against Iran-backed militias.

February 8, 2024

Justice Department declines to prosecute

Special counsel from the Department of Justice releases a report and declines to prosecute President Biden for mishandling classified documents after his vice presidency, but the report personally attacks the President, calling him "an elderly man with poor memory."

April 24, 2024

Aid to Ukraine, Israel, and Taiwan

President Joe Biden signs a $95.3 billion package of aid to Ukraine, Israel, and Taiwan, after months of debate in Congress led to a delay in approving the package.

June 4, 2024

Executive order to limit migrants

President Biden issues an executive order limiting asylum seekers at the US border. The order blocks migrants from crossing into the United States seeking asylum if the number of asylum seekers is more than 2,500 per day.

June 11, 2024

Hunter Biden found guilty

President Biden's son Hunter is found guilty on three counts of lying on a federal application for a firearm.

June 27, 2024

Disasterous debate

In the first debate of the 2024 presidential election, President Biden turns in a disasterous performance that leaves many questioning his ability to campaign for reelection.

July 13, 2024

Assassination attempt on Trump

At a rally in Pennsylvania, a gunman attempts to assassinate former President Donald Trump. He is grazed on his ear, but survives with no serious injuries. A spectator at the rally is killed, and two people are seriously injured.

July 21, 2024

Withdrawing from the campaign

In a letter posted on social media, President Biden announces that he will not seek reelection and will withdraw from the 2024 presidential campaign. He endorses Vice President Kamala Harris.

August 1, 2024

Prisoner swap

President Biden announces a prisoner swap with Russia, resulting in the return of 16 people in exchange for 8 Russians.

August 15, 2024

Lower drug prices

President Biden and Vice President Harris announce an agreement with major pharmaceutical companies to lower prices on widely used prescription drugs.

August 19, 2024

Democratic National Convention

President Biden speaks at the Democratic National Convention in Chicago, Illinois. Two days later on August 21, Vice President Kamala Harris accepts the Democratic nomination for president.

November 5, 2024

Election Day

Former President Donald Trump win

[Joe Biden](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden "Joe Biden")'s tenure as the [46th](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_presidents_of_the_United_States "List of presidents of the United States") [president of the United States](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States "President of the United States") began with [his inauguration](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inauguration_of_Joe_Biden "Inauguration of Joe Biden") on January 20, 2021, and ended on January 20, 2025. Biden, a member of the [Democratic Party](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Party_(United_States) "Democratic Party (United States)"), had previously served as the [47th vice president from 2009 to 2017](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_presidency_of_Joe_Biden "Vice presidency of Joe Biden") under President [Barack Obama](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama "Barack Obama"), took office after defeating the [Republican](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_Party_(United_States) "Republican Party (United States)") incumbent president [Donald Trump](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump") in the [2020 presidential election](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election "2020 United States presidential election"). Upon his inauguration, he became the [oldest president in American history](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_presidents_of_the_United_States_by_age "List of presidents of the United States by age"), breaking the record set by [Ronald Reagan](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Reagan "Ronald Reagan").[[1]](#cite_note-1) Alongside Biden's presidency, the Democratic Party also held their majorities in the [House of Representatives](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_House_of_Representatives "United States House of Representatives") and the [Senate](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate "United States Senate") during the [117th U.S. Congress](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/117th_United_States_Congress "117th United States Congress") following the [2020 elections](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_elections "2020 United States elections"), thereby attained an overall federal [government trifecta](about://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_trifecta#United_States "Government trifecta"). Biden entered office amid the [COVID-19 pandemic](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States "COVID-19 pandemic in the United States"), an [economic crisis](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_impact_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States "Economic impact of the COVID-19 pandemic in the United States"), and increased [political polarization](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_polarization_in_the_United_States "Political polarization in the United States").[[2]](#cite_note-2)

Day one actions of his presidency included restoring U.S. participation in the [Paris Agreement](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris_Agreement "Paris Agreement"), revoking the permit for the [Keystone XL](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keystone_XL "Keystone XL") pipeline and halting funding for the [Mexico–United States border wall](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexico–United_States_border_wall "Mexico–United States border wall").[[3]](#cite_note-Everett-2022-3) On his second day, he issued a series of executive orders to reduce the impact of [COVID-19](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19 "COVID-19"), including invoking the [Defense Production Act of 1950](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Defense_Production_Act_of_1950 "Defense Production Act of 1950"), and set an early goal of achieving one hundred million [COVID-19 vaccinations](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_vaccine "COVID-19 vaccine") in the United States in his first 100 days.[[4]](#cite_note-Klein-2021-4) The first major legislation signed into law by Biden was the [Amer

Contents of https://www.cfr.org/articles/bidens-legacy-major-accomplishments-unfinished-business:
*President Joe Biden ends his bid for reelection having revived American leadership in Asia and Europe and secured significant investments in the domestic economy, but his achievements will only last if his successor picks up where he leaves off.*

*Charles Kupchan is a senior fellow and professor of international affairs at Georgetown University. From 2014 to 2017, he served as special assistant to the president and senior director for European affairs on the staff of the National Security Council.*

President Joe Biden has faced a uniquely vexing task: navigating a fractured United States through a fractured world. Against this backdrop, his presidency has been one of remarkable accomplishment. Abroad, Biden restored the United States as the anchor of the free world while leading the successful effort to help Ukraine defend itself against Russian aggression. At home, he healed an economy that had been distressed by the pandemic and put the nation on a path of sustainable growth.

Yet as made clear by the divisiveness of the 2024 presidential race, Biden fell short of achieving his most ambitious objective: winning “[the battle for the soul of this nation](https://www.whitehouse.gov/briefing-room/speeches-remarks/2022/09/01/remarks-by-president-bidenon-the-continued-battle-for-the-soul-of-the-nation/ "the battle for the soul of this nation").” He came into office focused on the home front, determined to build back the middle class and ease the partisan divide. To this end, he successfully guided through a divided legislature [major domestic investments](https://www.npr.org/2023/01/01/1143149435/despite-infighting-its-been-a-surprisingly-productive-2-years-for-democrats "major domestic investments") aimed at promoting economic growth and getting working Americans back on their feet. But his efforts to get even more resources into the economic bloodstream were blocked by a recalcitrant Congress. Russia’s invasion of Ukraine then distracted him from his domestic agenda. Biden wanted four more years to finish the job of healing the nation. But that task now falls on the shoulders of the new Democratic nominee— most likely, Vice President Kamala Harris.

## Leader of Alliances

Biden reestablished the United States’ credentials as the world’s leading democracy and reclaimed the nation’s commitment to upholding a liberal international order. The United States’ image abroad, particularly among allies and partners, [sharply rebounded](https://www.pewresearch.org/global/2021/06/10/americas-image-abroad-rebounds-with-transition-from-trump-to-biden/ "sharply rebounded") almost overnight. Biden set about repairing relations with North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) allies, an effort that paid off handsomely after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Even before Russia launched its attack, he was laying the groundwork for the flow of military and economic assistance that enabled Ukraine to rebuff Russian efforts to subjugate the country. A stalemate has settled in, with Kyiv [still in control](https://www.cfr.org/expert-brief/what-happened-stalemate-ukraine "still in control") of some 80 percent of the country’s territory—a remarkable feat given Russia’s numerical superiority.

NATO today is strong and unified. Two-thirds of its members are now [meeting the benchmark](https://www.cfr.org/expert-brief/nato-countries-reach-spending-milestone-2-percent-enough "meeting the benchmark") of spending at least 2 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) on defense, up from only one-third of its membership in 2020. Finland and Sweden have joined the alliance, augmenting NATO’s aggregate strength and giving it new heft in the high north. The alliance can partly thank Russian President Vladimir Putin for this rebound, but Biden’s leadership in the face of Russian aggression has been steady and resolute.

The same goes for U.S. alliances in Asia. There is no counterpart to NATO in Asia, but to counter China’s growing strength and ambition Biden invested in a network of strategic partnerships with key countries, particularly Australia, India, Japan, and South Korea. He also strengthened deterrence by breaking with the tradition of “[strategic ambiguity](https://www.foreignaffairs.com/articles/united-states/american-support-taiwan-must-be-unambiguous "strategic ambiguity"),” confirming that the United States would defend Taiwan in the event of a Chinese attack. Once again, Biden exercised steady and resolute leadership. Chinese leader Xi Jinping has certainly taken notice, complaining that the United States is seeking to implement “[all-around containment, encirclement, and suppression against us](https://www.cfr.org/articles/how-read-xis-muscular-message-chinas-global-role "all-around containment, encirclement, and suppression against us").”

Biden has sustained criticism for providing [continuing support to Israel](https://www.cfr.org/articles/us-aid-israel-four-charts "continuing support to Israel") amid it

#### Story Highlights

WASHINGTON, D.C. -- During President Joe Biden’s third full year in office, spanning Jan. 20, 2023, to Jan. 19, 2024, an average of 39.8% of Americans approved of his job performance. Among prior presidents in the Gallup polling era who were elected to their first term, only Jimmy Carter fared worse in his third year. Carter averaged 37.4% approval in a year in which gas prices soared, inflation reached double digits and Iranian militants took U.S. citizens hostage.

Donald Trump, Barack Obama, Ronald Reagan, Bill Clinton and Richard Nixon also had sub-50% third-year averages. Dwight Eisenhower’s 72.1% is the highest for a third-year president.

###Embeddable###

Biden’s third-year average was lower than both his [first-year](https://news.gallup.com/poll/389033/biden-year-one-approval-ratings-subpar-extremely-polarized.aspx) (48.9%) and [second-year](https://news.gallup.com/poll/468806/biden-averaged-job-approval-second-year.aspx) (41.0%) averages. Though better than his third-year average, his first- and second-year ratings also ranked as the second lowest for recent presidents, ahead of only Trump in both years.

Biden registered new personal lows of 37% job approval in [April](https://news.gallup.com/poll/505202/biden-begins-reelection-bid-low-point-presidency.aspx), [October](https://news.gallup.com/poll/513305/democrats-ratings-biden-slip-overall-approval.aspx) and [November](https://news.gallup.com/poll/544808/poor-marks-biden-middle-east-economy-foreign-affairs.aspx) 2023 surveys.

Gallup’s latest job approval rating for Biden, from a Jan. 2-22 survey, is 41%, while 54% disapprove of how he is performing his job. Since [September 2021](https://news.gallup.com/poll/354872/biden-approval-rating-hits-new-low-harris.aspx), after the troubled withdrawal of U.S. troops from Afghanistan, Biden’s approval rating has ranged from the high 30s to low 40s. Before that, during the first six months of his presidency, he enjoyed majority-level approval ratings.

## **About Half of Recent Presidents Saw Improved Ratings in Fourth Year**

A key question for Biden, as he seeks reelection, is whether his job approval rating can be expected to improve this year. The historical evidence is mixed, based on a comparison of elected presidents’ third- and fourth-year job approval averages.

* Four presidents -- Nixon (+7 percentage points), Reagan (+11 points), Clinton (+8 points) and Obama (+4 points) -- saw meaningful improvement in their fourth year, and all four won reelection.
* Three presidents saw no significant change -- including the extremely popular Eisenhower, who won reelection, but also Carter and Trump, who were defeated for a second term.
* Two presidents -- George H.W. Bush and George W. Bush -- saw their approval ratings nosedive in their fourth year. The elder Bush lost his reelection bid after a 28-point drop, while the younger Bush, whose rating declined nine points, won.

###Embeddable###

The data indicate that presidents who successfully won reelection were close to -- or exceeded -- 50% approval during their fourth year in office.

## **Biden’s Ratings Continue to Be Among the Most Polarized**

During Biden’s third year in office, an average of 83% of Democrats and 5% of Republicans approved of the job he was doing, a 78-point party gap. Among third-year presidents, only Trump had greater party splits in his job approval ratings, averaging 82 points.

###Embeddable###

The increase in party polarization of presidential job approval ratings is underscored by the average 37-point partisan gap for presidents through the elder Bush, compared with 69 points for presidents in the past 30 years. This change has largely been fueled by increasingly lower job approval ratings from supporters of the opposition party, which now typically register in the single digits but were closer to 30% in the past.

Biden’s third-year party figures duplicate those from his second year in office and tie as the fifth most polarized annual average for any president. Trump’s fourth year, covering most of 2020 and early 2021, holds the record for the biggest average party gap in job approval ratings. That year, 91% of Republicans and 6% of Democrats approved of the job he was doing.

## 3. Critical / unfavorable evidence retained for balance

- **Persistently low approval.** Gallup's 2023 average of 39.8% is the second-worst third-year rating of any modern elected president (only Carter was lower). Independents hit a record-low 27% approval in November 2023 (Gallup, Dec 22 2023).
- **Polarization.** The 78-point partisan gap (83% D / 6% R) ties for the fifth largest in Gallup's historical series, signaling legitimacy and governing-coalition weakness.
- **Economic anxiety.** 68% of Americans said the economy was getting worse as 2023 closed; the top problem named by Americans was a tie between immigration and government (16% each), with the economy (14%) and inflation (12%) close behind (Gallup, Dec 2023).
- **Immigration crisis.** CFR notes ~2.5 million migrant encounters at the southern border in 2023 (up from 2.2 million in 2022), forcing Biden to pivot from more open policies to more restrictive measures despite Democratic mayors' pressure.
- **Israel–Gaza backlash.** After the Oct 7 Hamas attack killed ~1,200 Israelis and took ~250 hostages, Biden's full-throated support for Israel's military campaign drew sharp internal Democratic criticism; support among voters under 35 collapsed, and progressive Democrats publicly broke with the administration by year's end.
- **Special-counsel investigation.** Robert Hur's classified-documents investigation hung over Biden throughout 2023 (though the report exonerating him on charges only came in February 2024).
- **Age and fitness questions.** Biden turned 81 on Nov 20, 2023, the oldest sitting U.S. president. Polling throughout 2023 showed age as a top-three voter concern.

## 4. Favorable evidence retained for balance

- **Legislative productivity through a divided Congress.** The Fiscal Responsibility Act was a notable compromise with a Republican House; the Office of Gun Violence Prevention was the first federal office of its kind; the AI executive order was the most ambitious national AI framework to date; CHIPS and IRA implementation continued (Intel, TSMC, Micron fabs broke ground through 2023).
- **Foreign-policy leadership.** Wartime visit to Kyiv (Feb 20); sustained Ukraine military aid; Finland (April 2023) and Sweden (2024) joining NATO; expanded G7/G20/Quad engagement; Biden–Xi meeting at APEC (Nov 15, 2023); restraint after the Chinese balloon incident.
- **Labor and economic recovery signals.** 517,000 jobs added in January 2023; unemployment ~3.4–3.7% across most of 2023; wage growth outpacing inflation by Q4; gas-price decline; stock market near record highs by December.
- **Crisis response.** Rapid disaster declaration and federal mobilization for the Maui wildfire (Aug 8–21, 2023); active engagement with striking UAW workers (Sep 26, the first sitting president on a picket line); immediate support to Israel while pressing for humanitarian pauses.
